committed improper practices, acts of misbehaviours and falsification or
alteration of documents and providing false information within the meaning
of Articles 5.1, 5.2, 9.9, 10.2, 10.4 and 15.1 e) of the Integrity Code.
42. In this regard the Adjudicatory Body considers that the Respondent's
admission is self-evident and adequate to corroborate the violation. Indeed,
the Respondent has candidly confessed to falsifying flight tickets and
pursued personal interests during his tenure.
43. Furthermore, by failing to reimburse the athletes' families for all travel
expenses they incurred for their participation in competitions and
threatening to exclude them from competitions, the Respondent committed
acts of misbehaviours within the meaning of Articles 5.1 and 5.2 of the
Integrity Code.
44. The failure to reimburse the travel expenses has inflicted hardship for the
athletes and their families who had to bear the costs themselves to
participate in competitions, expenses that were supposed to be covered by
the FHSA. Moreover, the actions of the Respondent, such as requesting
reimbursements for non-existent athletes’ flights, further exacerbate the
violations committed and the consequences on the athletes. Such deceitful
practices not only betray the trust of the athletes but also tarnish the
integrity of the FHSA and the governing body responsible for upholding its
principles.
45. Also in this regard, the Adjudicatory Body considers that the Respondent’s
admission, together with the e-mail he sent to Mrs. Grand’Pierre on 30
January 2024, is self-evident and adequate to corroborate the violation.
46. The Respondent justified his actions by explaining that the FHSA faced
financial challenges due to the absence of membership and participation

fees and the lack of financial support from the Haitian Olympic Committee.
In an attempt to obtain additional funds for the FHSA, he invented expenses
and sought contributions from Haitian parents abroad.
47. He further explained that in his email of 30 January 2024, his main intention
was to address Mrs. Grand'Pierre, as she has a habit of contacting the
Haitian Olympic Committee and the Haitian Ministry of Sport on behalf of the
FHSA without due authorisation.
48. The Adjudicatory Body, while acknowledging the commendable admission of
the charges, considers that these arguments are neither a valid reason nor a
justification that could excuse such serious and condemnable behaviour as
tampering with invoices and threatening athletes. In this connection, the
Adjudicatory Body notes that Haitian Olympic Committee stopped subsidies
to the FHSA because it was suspended due to the irresponsible actions of
the FHSA officials.
49. In addition, the Respondent admitted using the electronic signatures of the
FHSA President and of the FHSA Treasurer without their approval, resulting
in the creation of unauthorised documents within the FHSA.
50. In this respect, the Adjudicatory Body notes that this explanation is irrelevant
as well as not credible as the 2021 and 2022 OASP Final Financial Report
and the 2023 Confirmation Form World Aquatics Support Programme were
signed with a handwritten signature and not with an electronic signature.
51. In light of the foregoing, the Adjudicatory Body deems that the Respondent
violated Articles 5.1, 5.2, 9.9, 10.2, 10.4 and 15.1 e) of the Integrity Code.
D. Applicable sanction
52. As per Article 33.1 of the Integrity Code, any one or more of the following
sanctions may be imposed for an Integrity Code Violation:
a) a warning as to future conduct;
b) a reprimand;
c) a fine in an amount proportionate to the seriousness of the violation;
d) an order of reimbursement or restitution;
e) a suspension from carrying out specific activities on behalf of World
Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World Aquatics Member
for a specified period;
f) a period of ineligibility, the length of which is to be determined based on
what is proportionate in the circumstances of the case, taking into
account in particular (i) the nature of the violation(s), (ii) the degree of fault
of the Covered Person, (iii) the harm that the violation(s) has/have done to
the sport, (iv) the need to deter future violations, and (v) any specific
aggravating or mitigating factors; and
g) any other sanction deemed appropriate, including, but not limited to
disqualification of results, annulment of results of any Event, removal

from office, forfeiture of points and/or of quota places and/or of hosting
rights, other loss of privileges, no contact directives, requirement to
complete educational or other programs, and return of World Aquatics
awards.
53. In this case, after considering (i) the nature of the violations, (ii) the degree of
fault of the Respondent, (iii) the harm that the violations have done to the
sport, (iv) the need to deter future violations and (v) any specific aggravating
or mitigating factors, the Adjudicatory Body has decided to impose a ten-
year suspension against the Respondent from taking part in any Aquatic-
related activities on behalf of World Aquatics and/or Continental
Organisation and/or World Aquatics Member.
54. The Respondent’s repeated violation of the Integrity Code cannot be taken
lightly. The Respondent is an experienced official and a former Executive
Director of a World Aquatics Member.
55. The Respondent further committed the above-described conduct in full
knowledge at the expense of World Aquatics and to the detriment of the
FHSA athletes.
56. As widely demonstrated indeed, the Respondent admitted to having
produced tampered invoices in order to receive the subsidies of the OASP
and also to deny athletes reimbursement for all travel expenses incurred for
their participation in competitions.
57. Therefore, the Respondent’s conduct must be condemned in every way,
especially in view of the position he holds in Aquatics.
58. With respect to the length of the period of ineligibility, the Adjudicatory Body
notes that in a similar case of tampering with invoices in order to request
reimbursements from World Aquatics committed by the former President of
the Chilean Swimming Federation, the Adjudicatory Body imposed a 20-
year suspension on him.1
59. Considering the above, the Adjudicatory Body is convinced that also in this
case it is paramount to issue a significant sanction to prevent such conduct
in the future and impose on the Respondent a suspension for a fixed period
of ten (10) years from taking part in any Aquatic-related activities on behalf
of World Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World Aquatics
Member.
60. The suspension imposed on the Respondent shall also prevent him from
attending in any capacity, any aquatics International Competition, as defined
at Article 2.2 of the World Aquatics Competition Regulations. For the sake of
clarity, the Olympic Games fall within the definition of International
Competition.
1 https://aquaticsintegrity.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/2024.02.29-Decision-of-the-AQIU-
Adjudicatory-Body-re-Marcos-JARA.pdf
See also: CAS 2019/A/6344 Marco Polo Del Nero v. Fédération Internationale de Football
Association (FIFA) and CAS 2018/A/6072 Kwesi Nyantakyi v. Fédération Internationale de Football
Association (FIFA)

61. Finally, the Adjudicatory Body observes that as per Article 21 of the Integrity
Code, the Respondent is as of 6 February 2024 provisionally suspended on
the ground that public confidence in the integrity of the sport of Aquatics is
at risk.
62. In this regard, the Adjudicatory Body notes that the suspension imposed
should be credited for the months during which the Respondent was
provisionally suspended, thus the ten-year suspension shall be effective
from the date in which the Respondent was provisionally suspended.

V. DECISION OF THE ADJUDICATORY BODY
(i) The AQIU has jurisdiction over this matter.
(ii) The Respondent has violated Articles 5.1, 5.2, 9.9, 10.2, 10.4 and
15.1 e) of the Integrity Code.
(iii) The Respondent is sanctioned with a 10-year period of ineligibility
from taking part in any Aquatic-related activities on behalf of
World Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World
Aquatics Member and/or recognised body. The sanction begins on
the day in which the Respondent was provisionally suspended, i.e.
6 February 2024.
(iv) This decision is rendered without costs.
(v) As per Article 35 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code, this decision
can be appealed to CAS within twenty-one (21) calendar days of
the appealing Party’s receipt of the written reasoned decision in
question by email.
On behalf of the Panel of the Adjudicatory Body of the Aquatics Integrity Unit:
Anna Peniche Raymond Hack Alexandre Miguel Mestre
Member Chairperson Member

title: 2024.08.06 AQIU Adjudicatory Body decision re Mr. Remilus HAI
text:
DECISION OF THE
ADJUDICATORY BODY
As per Article 32.3 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code
Decision by:
Raymond Hack (South Africa), Chairperson
Anna Peniche (Mexico), Member
Alexandre Miguel Mestre (Portugal), Member
In the matter related to:
Mr. Jean Jean Remilus (Haiti), Respondent
Regarding:
Article 5 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code - Duties of good conduct
Article 9 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code - Duty of undivided loyalty
Article 10 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code - Falsification and misuse of
funds
Article 15 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code - Anti-corruption rules
Lausanne, 6 August 2024
* * * * *

I. Overview
1. The present case relates to the conduct of the Treasurer of the Haitian
Federation of the Aquatic Sports (“FHSA”) Mr. Jean Jean Remilus (the
“Respondent” or “Mr. Remilus”).
2. More precisely, the Respondent has been charged by the Chief Ethics and
Compliance Officer (the “CECO”) of the Aquatics Integrity Unit (“AQIU”) with
committing a violation of the World Aquatics Integrity Code (“Integrity Code”)
in relation to his involvement in activities in breach of the World Aquatics
regulatory framework, occurred within the FHSA. In this context, a parallel
case has been opened against the FHSA President, Mr. Evenel Mervilus, the
FHSA Executive Director, Mr. James Cius and the FHSA administrator and
adjunct treasurer, Mrs. Ruby King for similar infringements.
II. Factual background
3. The following summary of the facts does not purport to include every single
contention put forth by the parties during these proceedings. However, the
Adjudicatory Body of the AQIU has thoroughly considered any and all
evidence and arguments submitted, even if no specific or detailed reference
has been made to those arguments in the following outline of its positions
and in the ensuing discussion on the merits.
4. Prior to his provisional suspension, the Respondent was the treasurer of the
FHSA.
5. In his capacity as treasurer of the FHSA, the Respondent was responsible for
the management of the FHSA’s finances and funds.
6. In 2021, 2022 and 2023, World Aquatics, through the Olympic Aquatics
Support Programme (“OASP”), remitted to the FHSA more than USD
75,000. The purpose of this program was to provide financial support to all
of World Aquatics National Member Federations (“MFs”) in their endeavours
to develop and foster aquatics at all levels within their territories including
covering the athletes' travel expenses.
7. In order to receive the financial support, each MFs had to submit a final
financial report (“OASP Final Financial Report”), documenting all expenses
incurred. The OASP Final Financial Report had to be signed by the
President/General Secretary and by the Treasurer/Head of finance of the
MF.
8. By signing the OASP Final Financial Report, the Respondent committed to
follow the Rules & Regulations of the OASP and certified that the
information provided was a true summary of the expenditure expected to be
associated with the organisation of the projects related to the National
Federation’s OASP.
9. On 16 September 2021, the Respondent signed the 2021 OASP Final
Financial Report. As proof of the incurred expenses, flight ticket receipts
from the travel agency “Lounair” were attached to the 2021 OASP Final
Financial Report.
10. On 2 August 2022, the Respondent signed the 2022 OASP Final Financial

Report. As proof of the incurred expenses, flight ticket receipts from the
travel agency “Lounair” were attached to the 2022 OASP Final Financial
Report.
11. For 2023, Mrs. Ruby King as a representative of the FHSA, in line with the
new dispositions of World Aquatics, filed the 2023 OASP Final Report Form.
Also in this case, as proof of the incurred expenses, flight ticket receipts
from the travel agency “Lounair” were attached.
12. On 23 February 2023, the President of the FHSA signed the Confirmation
Form World Aquatics Support Programme 2023. By signing this document,
the President of the FHSA committed to follow the World Aquatics Rules
and certified that the projects and objectives were approved by its Board of
Director or equivalent body - which includes the Respondent - and that the
information provided was a true summary of the expenditure expected to be
associated with the organisation of the projects related to the World
Aquatics Support Programme 2023.
III. Procedural background
a. Preliminary procedure before the CECO
13. On 26 January 2024, the President, Mr. Hans Larsen and the Secretary
General, Mr. Patrick Blanchet of the Haitian Olympic Committee lodged a
complaint (the "Complaint") against the Respondent, the FHSA President,
Mr. Evenel Mervilus and the FHSA administrator and adjunct treasurer, Mrs.
Ruby King with World Aquatics - requesting it to forward it to the AQIU. The
object of the Complaint was the financial mismanagement of the World
Aquatics funds granted to the FHSA to cover athletes’ travel costs for
competitions, which were not used as intended or communicated.
14. In this context, it was reported that the athletes’ families have incurred all
travel expenses for their participation in the competitions, without any
reimbursement from the FHSA, and that the latter threatened the athletes
and their parents with banning them from FHSA events if they approached
“FINA or World Aquatics, the Olympic Committee or the Ministry of Sports”.
Finally, it was also mentioned that some payments were made by the
athletes or their parents not to the FHSA account, but directly to the
account of the daughter of Treasurer Mervilus.
15. On 2 February 2024, the CECO decided to open proceedings against the
Respondent for possible violations of:
i. Article C.4 of the FINA Code of Ethics which prohibits “corrupt
practices”.
ii. Article 2 (a) of the FINA Code of Conduct which prohibits “acts of
misbehaviours”.
iii. Article 2 (b) of the FINA Code of Conduct which prohibits “falsification
or alteration of documents and providing false information”.
iv. Article 5 of the Integrity Code - Duties of good conduct
5.1 Covered Persons must always act honestly, fairly, impartially and in

accordance with the highest ethical standards of integrity and
transparency.
5.2 Covered Persons must avoid any conduct that is inconsistent with
or that undermines in any way the objectives of this Integrity Code.
v. Article 9 of the Integrity Code - Duty of undivided loyalty
9.9 Covered Persons must not abuse their position within Aquatics in
any way, especially for their own aims or objectives.
vi. Article 10 of the Integrity Code - Falsification and misuse of funds
10.2 Covered Persons must not knowingly give false information,
including false results, nationality and/or date of birth.
10.4 Covered Persons shall not misappropriate or misuse funds,
whether directly or indirectly through, or in conjunction with, third
parties. Covered Persons must use the resources of the World
Aquatics, Continental Organisations or World Aquatics Members only
for lawful and ethical purposes authorised by the relevant body.
16. On 3 February 2024, the Respondent denied all allegations against him,
stating that the FHSA had to face several challenges as it did not receive
any funds from the Haitian Olympic Committee. In addition, the Respondent
referred that one of the mothers' athletes, Mrs. Grand'Pierre, would have
worked for the FHSA and raised funds for it through the company Sons and
Daughters of Haiti even after her contract with the FHSA had not been
renewed.
17. On 5 February 2024, the Respondent sent a second email enclosing a copy
of the contract between the company Sons and Daughters of Haiti and the
FHSA, complaining of discrepancies with respect to the execution of the
contract.
18. On 6 February 2024, the CECO, pending the outcome of the investigation,
decided to impose a provisional suspension on the Respondent given that
public confidence in the integrity of the sport of Aquatics is at risk.
19. The provisional suspension has been effective from 6 February 2024 and
prevents Respondent from participating in any Aquatics-related activity,
including acting as Treasurer of a World Aquatics Member Federation.
20. From February to mid-April 2024, as part of the preliminary investigation,
the AQIU questioned and had several exchanges with Mrs. Grand'Pierre, who
reported that the FHSA did not reimburse athletes' travel expenses and
threatened to exclude them from competitions when they raised concerns
about it.
b. Main procedure before the CECO
21. On 17 April 2024, the CECO decided to formally charge the Respondent by
means of a notice of charge for possible violations of:
i. Article C.4 of the FINA Code of Ethics which prohibits “corrupt

practices”.
ii. Article 2 (a) of the FINA Code of Conduct which prohibits “acts of
misbehaviours”.
iii. Article 2 (b) of the FINA Code of Conduct which prohibits “falsification
or alteration of documents and providing false information”.
iv. Article 5 of the Integrity Code - Duties of good conduct
5.1 Covered Persons must always act honestly, fairly, impartially and in
accordance with the highest ethical standards of integrity and
transparency.
5.2 Covered Persons must avoid any conduct that is inconsistent with
or that undermines in any way the objectives of this Integrity Code.
v. Article 9 of the Integrity Code - Duty of undivided loyalty
9.9 Covered Persons must not abuse their position within Aquatics in
any way, especially for their own aims or objectives.
vi. Article 10 of the Integrity Code - Falsification and misuse of funds
10.2 Covered Persons must not knowingly give false information,
including false results, nationality and/or date of birth.
10.4 Covered Persons shall not misappropriate or misuse funds,
whether directly or indirectly through, or in conjunction with, third
parties. Covered Persons must use the resources of the World
Aquatics, Continental Organisations or World Aquatics Members only
for lawful and ethical purposes authorised by the relevant body.
vii. Article 15 of the Integrity Code - Anti-corruption Rules
15.1 Each of the following, when committed by a Covered Person
(whether directly or indirectly through any third group), will constitute
an Integrity Code Violation by that Covered Person:
[…]
e) Committing any act not otherwise prohibited under this Integrity
Code that amounts to a violation of any applicable criminal or other law
or regulation where such violation could undermine public confidence
in the integrity of an Event or the sport of Aquatics generally.
22. According to the Notice of Charge, the CECO determined that a ban of 20
years from participating in any Aquatics-related activities on behalf of World
Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World Aquatics Member,
should be the applicable disciplinary measure in this case.
23. Furthermore, the Respondent was also informed that in accordance with
Article 23.3 of the Integrity Code, he may respond to the Notice of Charge in
one of the following ways:

a. Admit the charge and accept a twenty-year ban from taking part in any
aquatics-related activity;
b. Admit the charge, but dispute and/or seek to mitigate all or any of the
potential consequences and have the Adjudicatory Body determine the
consequences and sanctions; or
c. Deny the charge, and have the Adjudicatory Body determine the
charge and any consequences and sanctions.
24. In his submissions of 19 April 2024, the Respondent denied all allegations
against him, asserting that the accusations were made considering only the
facts at hand, but not the context in which the FHSA operated, especially in
an unstable country like Haiti. He questioned the credibility of the allegations
made by the FHSA Executive Director, Mr. James Cius, pointing to instances
of misconduct and lack of transparency on his part. The Respondent
repeated the FHSA's relentless commitment despite the obstacles and
financial constraints imposed by the country's instability and criticised the
perceived unfair treatment of the Haitian Olympic Committee and World
Aquatics. He also questioned the independence of the AQIU, and threatened
to initiate legal action should the bias persist. Finally, he invited the President
of the FHSA to suspend participation in the World Aquatics events, he
demanded prompt reimbursement of expenses for the World Aquatics
Championships in Doha and for the CARIFTA 2024 and he threatened to
send the correspondence to all 208 MFs.
c. Procedure before the Adjudicatory Body
25. On 30 May 2024, the CECO referred the matter to the Adjudicatory Body. In
this regard, the CECO found that after thorough analysis of the documents
on file and in the light of all the new relevant information received, there
would appear to be no substantial indication that the conduct of the
Respondent would have violated Article C.4 of the FINA Code of Ethics and
Articles 2 (a) and 2 (b) of the FINA Code of Conduct. Having clarified this, the
CECO still found that the Respondent's conduct falls within the provisions of
the Integrity Code.
26. On 31 May 2024, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body, afforded the
Respondent an opportunity to provide his position on the matter.
27. On 5 June 2024, the Respondent denied all the charges by stating that he
acted professionally, following the directives of Mr. James Cius, who was
directing all operations ad that the AQIU relied on misunderstandings and
misinformation, for which he requested a second investigation by another
department.
28. On 13 June 2024, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body clarified that the Panel
has not yet adjudicated the matter and that, according to Article 29 of the
Integrity Code, the Panel feels sufficiently informed and does not consider a
hearing necessary.
29. On 7 July 2024, the Respondent reiterated his innocence and argued that
since Mr. James Cius admitted his guilt, it would be unfair to impose
suspensions on other innocent individuals. He then called for
reconsideration and for issuing a warning or minor sanction for Mr. James

Cius and no sanction for other individuals.
IV. CONSIDERATIONS OF THE ADJUDICATORY BODY
A. Jurisdiction, applicability of the Integrity Code and request for a hearing
30. In accordance with Article 24 of the Integrity Code, the Adjudicatory Body of
the AQIU is responsible for adjudicating cases where a respondent has
denied the charges or requests laid by the CECO.
31. The above shows that the AQIU, and, more precisely, the Adjudicatory Body,
has jurisdiction over the case and is entitled to pass a decision on the basis
of the Integrity Code.
32. The Adjudicatory Body took note that the Respondent did not request that a
hearing be held in this matter. In this regard, Article 29.1 of the Integrity Code
clearly states that the Adjudicatory Body has full discretion to decide
whether or not a hearing shall be convened. In this case, as already detailed
in the letter of 13 June 2024 from the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body to the
Respondent, the Adjudicatory Body considers itself sufficiently informed to
render a decision based on the written submissions. In coming to this
conclusion, the Adjudicatory Body noted the fact that the Respondent was
afforded several opportunities to provide his position on this matter by the
CECO and the Adjudicatory Body.
B. Burden and Standard of proof
33. The above having been established, the Adjudicatory Body recalled that, as
a general rule, the AQIU will have the burden of establishing that an Integrity
Code Violation has been committed.
34. The standard of proof will be the balance of probabilities. Facts shall be
established by any reliable means. The Panel shall at its own discretion
determine the admissibility, relevance, materiality and weight of the
evidence offered.
35. The principle of strict liability applies. Therefore, violations are punishable
regardless of whether they have been committed intentionally, recklessly,
and/or negligently.
36. Having clarified the foregoing, the Adjudicatory Body proceeded to consider
the merits of the case.
C. Merits of the case
37. Articles 5.1 and 5.2 of the Integrity Code:
“5.1 Covered Persons must always act honestly, fairly, impartially and in
accordance with the highest ethical standards of integrity and
transparency”.
“5.2 Covered Persons must avoid any conduct that is inconsistent with or
that undermines in any way the objectives of this Integrity Code”.
38. Article 9.9 of the Integrity Code:

“9.9 Covered Persons must not abuse their position within Aquatics in any
way, especially for their own aims or objectives”.
39. Articles 10.2 and 10.04 of the Integrity Code:
“10.2 Covered Persons must not knowingly give false information, including
false results, nationality and/or date of birth”.
“10.4 Covered Persons shall not misappropriate or misuse funds, whether
directly or indirectly through, or in conjunction with, third parties. Covered
Persons must use the resources of the World Aquatics, Continental
Organisations or World Aquatics Members only for lawful and ethical
purposes authorised by the relevant body”.
40. Article 15.1 e) of the Integrity Code:
“15.1 Each of the following, when committed by a Covered Person (whether
directly or indirectly through any third group), will constitute an Integrity
Code Violation by that Covered Person:
e) Committing any act not otherwise prohibited under this Integrity Code
that amounts to a violation of any applicable criminal or other law or
regulation where such violation could undermine public confidence in the
integrity of an Event or the sport of Aquatics generally”.
41. After review of the full case file, the Adjudicatory Body considers it has been
established that the conduct of the Respondent falls under these provisions.
42. In this regard, the Adjudicatory Body recalls that, as per definition of the
Integrity Code, a violation of the Integrity Code could also occur when a
Covered Person authorises, causes, or knowingly assists, encourages, aids
and abets, covers up, or is otherwise complicit in, any act or omission by any
person that would amount to a breach of any requirement of this Integrity
Code if committed by the Covered Person themself.
43. Since the Respondent was active as treasurer within the FHSA, he falls
within the definition of a “Covered Person” under Article 4.1 a) of the Integrity
Code.
44. By submitting tampered flight ticket receipts and providing false information
for the purpose of receiving funds from the OASP, the Respondent
committed omissions, acts of misbehaviours, falsification or alteration of
documents and providing false information and indirectly misusing funds
within the meaning of Articles 5.1, 5.2, 9.9, 10.2, 10.4 and 15.1 e) of the
Integrity Code.
45. In this regard the Adjudicatory Body notes that the flight ticket receipts
submitted to World Aquatics present graphical and typographical
inaccuracies, as well as inconsistencies concerning flight times, dates and
passengers.
46. Typically, flight ticket receipts are automatically generated, with
standardised fonts and formatting. However, in this case, they have
noticeable typographical anomalies, such as inconsistent characters,

spacing irregularities and deviations from the standard format. These
anomalies also raise several doubts as to the existence of the Lounair travel
agency which issued all the flight tickets.
47. In confirmation of this, is the statement of Mr. Cius in his email of 18 April
2024 who admitted to having altered documents including airline tickets.
48. In this respect, the Respondent argued that he was not responsible as he
acted professionally, following the directives of Mr. James Cius, who was
directing all operations and that that the FHSA has faced several challenges,
various obstacles and financial constraints due to the instability of the
country and criticised the unfair treatment of the Haitian Olympic
Committee as it stopped subsidising the FHSA.
49. The Adjudicatory Body considers that these arguments are neither a valid
reason nor a justification that could excuse such serious and condemnable
behaviour as tampering with invoices. The Respondent merely discharged
the responsibility onto other FHSA official. This, however, did not relieve him
of liability since he, as treasurer, has represented the FHSA and signed the
OASP Final Financial Report in 2021 and 2022 and the Confirmation Form
World Aquatics Support Programme in 2023.
50. By signing the OASP Final Financial Report, the Respondent committed to
follow the Rules & Regulations of the OASP and certified that the
information provided was a true summary of the expenditure expected to be
associated with the organisation of the projects related to the National
Federation’s OASP.
51. The Adjudicatory Body also notes that Haitian Olympic Committee stopped
subsidies to the FHSA because it was suspended due to the irresponsible
actions of the FHSA executives.
52. In light of the above, the Adjudicatory Body notes that the Respondent, by
signing the OASP Final Financial Reports to which the tampered invoices are
attached and in his capacity as treasurer of the FHSA, could not have been
unaware that the invoices were falsified, but rather was complicit in it. That
said, even if it were to be assumed that he was unaware of the facts, his
negligence does not exempt him from liability, since by signing the 2021 and
2022 OASP Final Financial Report, he was responsible for it.
53. Furthermore, by failing to reimburse the athletes’ families for all travel
expenses they incurred for their participation in competitions, the
Respondent was also complicit in acts of misbehaviours within the meaning
of Articles 5.1 and 5.2 of the Integrity Code.
54. The Adjudicatory Body notes that the Respondent made no comment in this
regard.
55. Nevertheless, the failure to reimburse the travel expenses has inflicted
severe hardship for the athletes and their families who had to bear the costs
themselves to participate in competitions, expenses that were supposed to
be covered by the FHSA. Moreover, the actions of the FHSA, such as
requesting reimbursements for non-existent athlete flights, further
exacerbate the injustice faced by the athletes. Such deceitful practices not
only betray the trust of the athletes but also tarnish the integrity of the

FHSA and the governing body responsible for upholding its principles.
56. Lasty, as some payments were made by athletes or their parents not to the
FHSA official bank account but directly to the account of the FHSA
President’s daughter, Ms. Lean Mervilus, the Respondent was also complicit
in acts of mismanagement and financial transparency within the meaning of
Article 5.1 of the Integrity Code.
57. In this respect, the Respondent argued that some of the FHSA funds were
transferred to the personal account of the FHSA President’s daughter due
to the difficulties there are in Haiti with banking transactions.
58. The Adjudicatory Body considers that this is not a valid reason to justify this
modus operandi but rather increases the convention that the Respondent
was complicit in a scheme of improper conduct within the FHSA. This
scheme revolved around the submission of fraudulent invoices; a practice
designed to take advantage of the OASP reimbursement system.
Specifically, the Respondent was complicit in submitting the tampered flight
tickets of the athletes. However, these reimbursements were requested for
expenses that were never actually incurred by the athletes themselves but
were falsely attributed to them. In this context, the fact that some of these
reimbursements were paid into the bank account of the FHSA President’s
daughter and that their destination remains shrouded in mystery, raises
serious concerns about potential misappropriation.
59. Furthermore, the Respondent raised doubts about the management of the
company Sons and Daughters of Haiti whose object was to raise funds to
help athletes cover their travel costs to participate in competitions. In this
regard, the Adjudicatory Body believes that these allegations are baseless
since they are not substantiated by any concrete evidence rather than
irrelevant as the crux of the matter concerns the mismanagement of funds
by the FHSA and its executives who are covered by the World Aquatics
regulations. The allegations made against a company that is independent
and thus not subject to the World Aquatics regulatory framework are
therefore without any merit.
60. The Respondent finally questioned the independence of the AQIU and
threatened to take legal action and to send his correspondence to all MFs.
61. In this regard, the Adjudicatory Body finds these arguments without any
merit and emphasises that the AQIU is an operationally independent body
which operates free from any external interventions.
62. In light of the foregoing, the Adjudicatory Body deems that the Respondent
violated Articles 5.1, 5.2, 9.9, 10.2, 10.4 and 15.1 e) of the Integrity Code.
D. Applicable sanction
63. As per Article 33.1 of the Integrity Code, any one or more of the following
sanctions may be imposed for an Integrity Code Violation:
a) a warning as to future conduct;
b) a reprimand;

c) a fine in an amount proportionate to the seriousness of the violation;
d) an order of reimbursement or restitution;
e) a suspension from carrying out specific activities on behalf of World
Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World Aquatics Member
for a specified period;
f) a period of ineligibility, the length of which is to be determined based on
what is proportionate in the circumstances of the case, taking into
account in particular (i) the nature of the violation(s), (ii) the degree of fault
of the Covered Person, (iii) the harm that the violation(s) has/have done to
the sport, (iv) the need to deter future violations, and (v) any specific
aggravating or mitigating factors; and
g) any other sanction deemed appropriate, including, but not limited to
disqualification of results, annulment of results of any Event, removal
from office, forfeiture of points and/or of quota places and/or of hosting
rights, other loss of privileges, no contact directives, requirement to
complete educational or other programs, and return of World Aquatics
awards.
64. In this case, after considering (i) the nature of the violations, (ii) the degree of
fault of the Respondent, (iii) the harm that the violations have done to the
sport, (iv) the need to deter future violations and (v) any specific aggravating
or mitigating factors, the Adjudicatory Body has decided to impose a ten-
year suspension against the Respondent from taking part in any Aquatic-
related activities on behalf of World Aquatics and/or Continental
Organisation and/or World Aquatics Member.
65. The Respondent’s violation of the Integrity Code cannot be taken lightly. The
Respondent is an experienced official and a former Treasurer of a World
Aquatics Member.
66. As per definition of the Integrity Code, a violation of the Integrity Code could
also occur when a Covered Person authorises, causes, or knowingly assists,
encourages, aids and abets, covers up, or is otherwise complicit in, any act or
omission by any person that would amount to a breach of any requirement
of this Integrity Code if committed by the Covered Person themself.
67. The Adjudicatory Body considers that the Respondent's conduct falls within
this case.
68. The Respondent was complicit in actions and omissions that were
committed in full knowledge at the expense of World Aquatics and to the
detriment of the FHSA athletes.
69. As widely demonstrated indeed, the Respondent was involved in
misconduct within the FHSA to submit to World Aquatics tampered invoices
in order to receive the subsidies of the OASP and also to deny athletes
reimbursement for all travel expenses incurred for their participation in
competitions.
70. Therefore, the Respondent’s conduct must be condemned in every way,
especially in view of the position he holds in Aquatics.

71. With respect to the length of the period of ineligibility, the Adjudicatory Body
notes that in a similar case of tampering with invoices in order to request
reimbursements from World Aquatics committed by the former President of
the Chilean Swimming Federation, the Adjudicatory Body imposed a 20-
year suspension on him.1
72. Considering the above, the Adjudicatory Body is convinced that also in this
case it is paramount to issue a significant sanction to prevent such conduct
in the future and impose on the Respondent a suspension for a fixed period
of ten (10) years from taking part in any Aquatic-related activities on behalf
of World Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World Aquatics
Member.
73. The suspension imposed on the Respondent shall also prevent him from
attending in any capacity, any aquatics International Competition, as defined
at Article 2.2 of the World Aquatics Competition Regulations. For the sake of
clarity, the Olympic Games fall within the definition of International
Competition.
74. Finally, the Adjudicatory Body observes that as per Article 21 of the Integrity
Code, the Respondent is as of 6 February 2024 provisionally suspended on
the ground that public confidence in the integrity of the sport of Aquatics is
at risk.
75. In this regard, the Adjudicatory Body notes that the suspension imposed
should be credited for the months during which the Respondent was
provisionally suspended, thus the ten-year suspension shall be effective
from the date in which the Respondent was provisionally suspended, i.e. 6
February 2024.
1 https://aquaticsintegrity.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/2024.02.29-Decision-of-the-AQIU-
Adjudicatory-Body-re-Marcos-JARA.pdf
See also: CAS 2019/A/6344 Marco Polo Del Nero v. Fédération Internationale de Football
Association (FIFA) and CAS 2018/A/6072 Kwesi Nyantakyi v. Fédération Internationale de Football
Association (FIFA)

V. DECISION OF THE ADJUDICATORY BODY
(i) The AQIU has jurisdiction over this matter.
(ii) The Respondent has violated Articles 5.1, 5.2, 9.9, 10.2, 10.4 and
15.1 e) of the Integrity Code.
(iii) The Respondent is sanctioned with a 10-year period of ineligibility
from taking part in any Aquatic-related activities on behalf of
World Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World
Aquatics Member and/or recognised body. The sanction begins on
the day in the Respondent was provisionally suspended, i.e. 6
February 2024.
(iv) This decision is rendered without costs.
(v) As per Article 35 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code, this decision
can be appealed to CAS within twenty-one (21) calendar days of
the appealing Party’s receipt of the written reasoned decision in
question by email.

title: 2024.08.06 AQIU Adjudicatory Body decision re Mrs. King HAI
text:
DECISION OF THE
ADJUDICATORY BODY
As per Article 32.3 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code
Decision by:
Raymond Hack (South Africa), Chairperson
Anna Peniche (Mexico), Member
Alexandre Miguel Mestre (Portugal), Member
In the matter related to:
Mrs. Ruby King (Haiti), Respondent
Regarding:
Article 5 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code - Duties of good conduct
Article 10 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code - Falsification and misuse of
funds
Article 15 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code - Anti-corruption rules
Lausanne, 6 August 2024
* * * * *

I. Overview
1. The present case relates to the conduct of the administrator and adjunct
treasurer of the FHSA of the Haitian Federation of the Aquatic Sports
(“FHSA”) Mrs. Ruby King (the “Respondent” or “Mrs. King”).
2. More precisely, the Respondent has been charged by the Chief Ethics and
Compliance Officer (the “CECO”) of the Aquatics Integrity Unit (“AQIU”) with
committing a violation of the World Aquatics Integrity Code (“Integrity Code”)
in relation to his involvement in activities in breach of the World Aquatics
regulatory framework, occurred within the FHSA. In this context, a parallel
case has been opened against the FHSA President, Mr. Evenel Mervilus, the
FHSA Executive Director, Mr. James Cius and the FHSA treasurer, Mr. Jean
Jean Remilus for similar infringements.
II. Factual background
3. The following summary of the facts does not purport to include every single
contention put forth by the parties during these proceedings. However, the
Adjudicatory Body of the AQIU has thoroughly considered any and all
evidence and arguments submitted, even if no specific or detailed reference
has been made to those arguments in the following outline of its positions
and in the ensuing discussion on the merits.
4. Prior to her provisional suspension, the Respondent was the administrator
and adjunct treasurer of the FHSA.
5. In her capacity as administrator and adjunct treasurer of the FHSA, the
Respondent was responsible for the management of the FHSA.
6. In 2021, 2022 and 2023, World Aquatics, through the OASP, remitted to the
FHSA more than USD 75,000. The purpose of this program was to provide
financial support to all of World Aquatics National Member Federations
("MFs") in their endeavours to develop and foster aquatics at all levels within
their territories including covering the athletes' travel expenses.
7. In order to receive the financial support, each MFs had to submit a final
financial report (“OASP Final Financial Report”), documenting all expenses
incurred. The OASP Final Financial Report had to be signed by the
President/General Secretary and by the Treasurer/Head of finance of the
MF.
8. By signing the OASP Final Financial Report, the President and the Treasurer
committed to follow the Rules & Regulations of the OASP and certified that
the information provided was a true summary of the expenditure expected
to be associated with the organisation of the projects related to the National
Federation’s OASP.
9. On 16 September 2021, the President and the treasurer of the FHSA signed
the 2021 OASP Final Financial Report. As proof of the incurred expenses,
flight ticket receipts from the travel agency “Lounair” were attached to the
2021 OASP Final Financial Report.
10. On 2 August 2022, the President and the treasurer of the FHSA signed the
2022 OASP Final Financial Report. As proof of the incurred expenses, flight

ticket receipts from the travel agency “Lounair” were attached to the 2022
OASP Final Financial Report.
11. For 2023, the Respondent as a representative of the FHSA, in line with the
new dispositions of World Aquatics, filed the 2023 OASP Final Report Form.
Also in this case, as proof of the incurred expenses, flight ticket receipts
from the travel agency “Lounair” were attached.
12. On 23 February 2023, the President of the FHSA signed the Confirmation
Form World Aquatics Support Programme 2023. By signing this document,
the Respondent committed to follow the World Aquatics Rules and certified
that the projects and objectives were approved by its Board of Director or
equivalent body - which includes the Respondent - and that the information
provided was a true summary of the expenditure expected to be associated
with the organisation of the projects related to the World Aquatics Support
Programme 2023.
III. Procedural background
a. Preliminary procedure before the CECO
13. On 26 January 2024, the President, Mr. Hans Larsen and the Secretary
General, Mr. Patrick Blanchet of the Haitian Olympic Committee lodged a
complaint (the "Complaint") against the Respondent, the FHSA President,
Mr. Evenel Mervilus and the FHSA treasurer, Mr. Jean Jean Remilus with
World Aquatics - requesting it to forward it to the AQIU. The object of the
Complaint was the financial mismanagement of the World Aquatics funds
granted to the FHSA to cover athletes’ travel costs for competitions, which
were not used as intended or communicated.
14. In this context, it was reported that the athletes’ families have incurred all
travel expenses for their participation in the competitions, without any
reimbursement from the FHSA, and that the latter threatened the athletes
and their parents with banning them from FHSA events if they approached
“FINA or World Aquatics, the Olympic Committee or the Ministry of Sports”.
Finally, it was also mentioned that some payments were made by the
athletes or their parents not to the FHSA account, but directly to the
account of the daughter of the FHSA President.
15. On 2 February 2024, the CECO decided to open proceedings against the
Respondent for possible violations of:
i. Article C.4 of the FINA Code of Ethics which prohibits “corrupt
practices”.
ii. Article 2 (a) of the FINA Code of Conduct which prohibits “acts of
misbehaviours”.
iii. Article 2 (b) of the FINA Code of Conduct which prohibits “falsification
or alteration of documents and providing false information”.
iv. Article 5 of the Integrity Code - Duties of good conduct
5.1 Covered Persons must always act honestly, fairly, impartially and in
accordance with the highest ethical standards of integrity and

transparency.
5.2 Covered Persons must avoid any conduct that is inconsistent with
or that undermines in any way the objectives of this Integrity Code.
v. Article 9 of the Integrity Code - Duty of undivided loyalty
9.9 Covered Persons must not abuse their position within Aquatics in
any way, especially for their own aims or objectives.
vi. Article 10 of the Integrity Code - Falsification and misuse of funds
10.2 Covered Persons must not knowingly give false information,
including false results, nationality and/or date of birth.
10.4 Covered Persons shall not misappropriate or misuse funds,
whether directly or indirectly through, or in conjunction with, third
parties. Covered Persons must use the resources of the World
Aquatics, Continental Organisations or World Aquatics Members only
for lawful and ethical purposes authorised by the relevant body.
16. On the same day, the Respondent denied all allegations against her, stating
that there was a communication gap between the FHSA and some of the
parents and friends associated with the FHSA and that, due to her health
problems, Mr. James Cius took on the responsibility of coordinating Haiti's
representation at the World Aquatics Championships in Doha. She then
asserted that the FSHA would have proceed to refund the athlete who was
denied reimbursement. Finally, in relation to the fact that some payments
were made by athletes or their parents not to the FHSA account but directly
to the account of the President’s daughter, Ms. Lean Mervilus, she stated
that this was due to circumstances beyond her control and the difficulties
there are in Haiti with banking transactions.
17. On 6 February 2024, the CECO, pending the outcome of the investigation,
decided to impose a provisional suspension on the Respondent given that
public confidence in the integrity of the sport of Aquatics is at risk.
18. The provisional suspension has been effective from 6 February 2024 and
prevents Respondent from participating in any Aquatics-related activity,
including acting as president of a World Aquatics Member Federation.
19. From February to mid-April 2024, as part of the preliminary investigation,
the AQIU questioned and had several exchanges with parent of the athletes,
who reported that the FHSA did not reimburse athletes' travel expenses and
threatened to exclude them from competitions when they raised concerns
about it.
b. Main procedure before the CECO
20. On 17 April 2024, the CECO decided to formally charge the Respondent by
means of a notice of charge for possible violations of:
i. Article C.4 of the FINA Code of Ethics which prohibits “corrupt
practices”.

ii. Article 2 (a) of the FINA Code of Conduct which prohibits “acts of
misbehaviours”.
iii. Article 2 (b) of the FINA Code of Conduct which prohibits “falsification
or alteration of documents and providing false information”.
iv. Article 5 of the Integrity Code - Duties of good conduct
5.1 Covered Persons must always act honestly, fairly, impartially and in
accordance with the highest ethical standards of integrity and
transparency.
5.2 Covered Persons must avoid any conduct that is inconsistent with
or that undermines in any way the objectives of this Integrity Code.
v. Article 9 of the Integrity Code - Duty of undivided loyalty
9.9 Covered Persons must not abuse their position within Aquatics in
any way, especially for their own aims or objectives.
vi. Article 10 of the Integrity Code - Falsification and misuse of funds
10.2 Covered Persons must not knowingly give false information,
including false results, nationality and/or date of birth.
10.4 Covered Persons shall not misappropriate or misuse funds,
whether directly or indirectly through, or in conjunction with, third
parties. Covered Persons must use the resources of the World
Aquatics, Continental Organisations or World Aquatics Members only
for lawful and ethical purposes authorised by the relevant body.
vii. Article 15 of the Integrity Code - Anti-corruption Rules
15.1 Each of the following, when committed by a Covered Person
(whether directly or indirectly through any third group), will constitute
an Integrity Code Violation by that Covered Person:
[…]
e) Committing any act not otherwise prohibited under this Integrity
Code that amounts to a violation of any applicable criminal or other law
or regulation where such violation could undermine public confidence
in the integrity of an Event or the sport of Aquatics generally.
21. According to the Notice of Charge, the CECO determined that a ban of 20
years from participating in any Aquatics-related activities on behalf of World
Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World Aquatics Member,
should be the applicable disciplinary measure in this case.
22. Furthermore, the Respondent was also informed that in accordance with
Article 23.3 of the Integrity Code, he may respond to the Notice of Charge in
one of the following ways:
a. Admit the charge and accept a twenty-year ban from taking part in any
aquatics-related activity;

b. Admit the charge, but dispute and/or seek to mitigate all or any of the
potential consequences and have the Adjudicatory Body determine the
consequences and sanctions; or
c. Deny the charge, and have the Adjudicatory Body determine the
charge and any consequences and sanctions.
23. In her submissions of 20 April 2024, the Respondent denied all allegations
against her and claimed to have no control over the individuals who engaged
in the falsification and therefore denied being involved in illicit activities.
c. Procedure before the Adjudicatory Body
24. On 30 May 2024, the CECO referred the matter to the Adjudicatory Body. In
this regard, the CECO found that after thorough analysis of the documents
on file and in the light of all the new relevant information received, there
would appear to be no substantial indication that the conduct of the
Respondent would have violated Article C.4 of the FINA Code of Ethics and
Articles 2 (a) and 2 (b) of the FINA Code of Conduct and Articles 9.9 and 10.4
of the Integrity Code. Having clarified this, the CECO still found that the
Respondent's conduct falls within the other provisions of the Integrity Code.
25. On 31 May 2024, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body, afforded the
Respondent an opportunity to provide her position on the matter.
26. On 2 June 2024, the Respondent denied all the charges and stated that
“AQIU does not have the moral authority to impose sanctions”.
27. On 13 June 2024, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body clarified that the Panel
has not yet adjudicated the matter and that, according to Article 29 of the
Integrity Code, the Panel feels sufficiently informed and does not consider a
hearing necessary.
28. On 30 June 2024, the Respondent requested an update on the
proceedings.
29. On 7 July 2024, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body confirmed that the
proceedings are still pending before the Adjudicatory Body of the AQIU. In
this context, because the Respondent violated the provisional suspension,
the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body sent her a reminder of obligation to
comply with the provisional suspension.
IV. CONSIDERATIONS OF THE ADJUDICATORY BODY
A. Jurisdiction, applicability of the Integrity Code and request for a hearing
30. In accordance with Article 24 of the Integrity Code, the Adjudicatory Body of
the AQIU is responsible for adjudicating cases where a respondent has
denied the charges or requests laid by the CECO.
31. The above shows that the AQIU, and, more precisely, the Adjudicatory Body,
has jurisdiction over the case and is entitled to pass a decision on the basis
of the Integrity Code.

32. The Adjudicatory Body took note that the Respondent did not request that a
hearing be held in this matter. In this regard, Article 29.1 of the Integrity Code
clearly states that the Adjudicatory Body has full discretion to decide
whether or not a hearing shall be convened. In this case, as already detailed
in the letter of 13 June 2024 from the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body to the
Respondent, the Adjudicatory Body considers itself sufficiently informed to
render a decision based on the written submissions. In coming to this
conclusion, the Adjudicatory Body noted the fact that the Respondent was
afforded several opportunities to provide his position on this matter by the
CECO and the Adjudicatory Body.
B. Burden and Standard of proof
33. The above having been established, the Adjudicatory Body recalled that, as
a general rule, the AQIU will have the burden of establishing that an Integrity
Code Violation has been committed.
34. The standard of proof will be the balance of probabilities. Facts shall be
established by any reliable means. The Panel shall at its own discretion
determine the admissibility, relevance, materiality and weight of the
evidence offered.
35. The principle of strict liability applies. Therefore, violations are punishable
regardless of whether they have been committed intentionally, recklessly,
and/or negligently.
36. Having clarified the foregoing, the Adjudicatory Body proceeded to consider
the merits of the case.
C. Merits of the case
37. Articles 5.1 and 5.2 of the Integrity Code:
“5.1 Covered Persons must always act honestly, fairly, impartially and in
accordance with the highest ethical standards of integrity and
transparency”.
“5.2 Covered Persons must avoid any conduct that is inconsistent with or
that undermines in any way the objectives of this Integrity Code”.
38. Article 10.2 of the Integrity Code:
“10.2 Covered Persons must not knowingly give false information, including
false results, nationality and/or date of birth”.
39. Article 15.1 e) of the Integrity Code:
“15.1 Each of the following, when committed by a Covered Person (whether
directly or indirectly through any third group), will constitute an Integrity
Code Violation by that Covered Person:
e) Committing any act not otherwise prohibited under this Integrity Code
that amounts to a violation of any applicable criminal or other law or
regulation where such violation could undermine public confidence in the
integrity of an Event or the sport of Aquatics generally”.

40. After review of the full case file, the Adjudicatory Body considers it has been
established that the conduct of the Respondent falls under these provisions.
41. In this regard, the Adjudicatory Body recalls that, as per definition of the
Integrity Code, a violation of the Integrity Code could also occur when a
Covered Person authorises, causes, or knowingly assists, encourages, aids
and abets, covers up, or is otherwise complicit in, any act or omission by any
person that would amount to a breach of any requirement of this Integrity
Code if committed by the Covered Person themself.
42. Since the Respondent was active as administrator and adjunct treasurer
within the FHSA, she falls within the definition of a “Covered Person” under
Article 4.1 a) of the Integrity Code.
43. By filing an official document with tampered flight ticket receipts and
providing false information for the purpose of receiving funds from the
OASP, the Respondent committed omissions, acts of misbehaviours and
falsification or alteration of documents and providing false information
within the meaning of Articles 5.1, 5.2, 10.2, and 15.1 e) of the Integrity Code.
44. In this regard the Adjudicatory Body notes that the flight ticket receipts
submitted to World Aquatics present graphical and typographical
inaccuracies, as well as inconsistencies concerning flight times, dates and
passengers.
45. Typically, flight ticket receipts are automatically generated, with
standardised fonts and formatting. However, in this case, they have
noticeable typographical anomalies, such as inconsistent characters,
spacing irregularities and deviations from the standard format. These
anomalies also raise several doubts as to the existence of the Lounair travel
agency which issued all the flight tickets.
46. In confirmation of this, is the statement of Mr. Cius in his email of 18 April
2024 who admitted to having altered documents including airline tickets.
47. In light of the above, the Adjudicatory Body notes that the Respondent, by
filing the 2023 OASP Final Report Form to which the tampered invoices
were attached and in her capacity as administrator and adjunct treasurer of
the FHSA, could not have been unaware that the invoices were falsified, but
rather was complicit in it. That said, even if it were to be assumed that she
was unaware of the facts, her negligence does not exempt her from liability,
since as administrator and adjunct treasurer she was responsible for the
management of the FHSA.
48. Furthermore, by failing to reimburse the athletes’ families for all travel
expenses they incurred for their participation in competitions, the
Respondent was also complicit in acts of misbehaviours within the meaning
of Articles 5.1 and 5.2 of the Integrity Code.
49. The failure to reimburse the travel expenses has inflicted severe hardship for
the athletes and their families who had to bear the costs themselves to
participate in competitions, expenses that were supposed to be covered by
the FHSA. Moreover, the actions of the FHSA, such as requesting
reimbursements for non-existent athlete flights, further exacerbate the

injustice faced by the athletes. Such deceitful practices not only betray the
trust of the athletes but also tarnish the integrity of the FHSA and the
governing body responsible for upholding its principles.
50. Lasty, as some payments were made by athletes or their parents not to the
FHSA official bank account but directly to the account of the daughter’s
President, Ms. Lean Mervilus, the Respondent as administrator and adjunct
treasurer of the FHSA, was also complicit in acts of mismanagement and
financial transparency within the meaning of Article 5.1 of the Integrity Code.
51. The Respondent only argued that she had no control over the individuals
who engaged in the falsification and denied being involved in illicit activities.
52. The Adjudicatory Body considers that these arguments are neither a valid
reason nor a justification that could excuse such serious and condemnable
behaviour as tampering with invoices. Indeed, the Adjudicatory Body is of
the opinion that, as administrator and adjunct treasurer of the FHSA, the
Respondent was responsible for the management of the finances of the
FHSA thus, she could not have been unaware of the mismanagement of the
FHSA's funds and even if this were the case, her negligence does not
exempt her from liability.
53. Instead, the Adjudicatory Body believes that the Respondent was complicit
in a scheme of improper conduct within the FHSA. This scheme revolved
around the submission of fraudulent invoices; a practice designed to take
advantage of the OASP reimbursement system. Specifically, the
Respondent was complicit in submitting the tampered flight tickets of the
athletes. However, these reimbursements were requested for expenses that
were never actually incurred by the athletes themselves but were falsely
attributed to them. Moreover, the destination of these wrongfully obtained
funds remains shrouded in mystery, raising serious concerns about potential
misappropriation.
54. In light of the foregoing, the Adjudicatory Body deems that the Respondent
violated Articles 5.1, 5.2, 10.2 and 15.1 e) of the Integrity Code.
D. Applicable sanction
55. As per Article 33.1 of the Integrity Code, any one or more of the following
sanctions may be imposed for an Integrity Code Violation:
a) a warning as to future conduct;
b) a reprimand;
c) a fine in an amount proportionate to the seriousness of the violation;
d) an order of reimbursement or restitution;
e) a suspension from carrying out specific activities on behalf of World
Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World Aquatics Member
for a specified period;
f) a period of ineligibility, the length of which is to be determined based on
what is proportionate in the circumstances of the case, taking into

account in particular (i) the nature of the violation(s), (ii) the degree of fault
of the Covered Person, (iii) the harm that the violation(s) has/have done to
the sport, (iv) the need to deter future violations, and (v) any specific
aggravating or mitigating factors; and
g) any other sanction deemed appropriate, including, but not limited to
disqualification of results, annulment of results of any Event, removal
from office, forfeiture of points and/or of quota places and/or of hosting
rights, other loss of privileges, no contact directives, requirement to
complete educational or other programs, and return of World Aquatics
awards.
56. In this case, after considering (i) the nature of the violations, (ii) the degree of
fault of the Respondent, (iii) the harm that the violations have done to the
sport, (iv) the need to deter future violations and (v) any specific aggravating
or mitigating factors, the Adjudicatory Body has decided to impose a five-
year suspension against the Respondent from taking part in any Aquatic-
related activities on behalf of World Aquatics and/or Continental
Organisation and/or World Aquatics Member.
57. The Respondent’s violation of the Integrity Code cannot be taken lightly. The
Respondent is an experienced official and a former administrator and
adjunct treasurer of a World Aquatics Member.
58. As per definition of the Integrity Code, a violation of the Integrity Code could
also occur when a Covered Person authorises, causes, or knowingly assists,
encourages, aids and abets, covers up, or is otherwise complicit in, any act or
omission by any person that would amount to a breach of any requirement
of this Integrity Code if committed by the Covered Person themself.
59. The Adjudicatory Body considers that the Respondent's conduct falls within
this case.
60. The Respondent was complicit in actions and omissions that were
committed in full knowledge at the expense of World Aquatics and to the
detriment of the FHSA athletes.
61. As widely demonstrated indeed, the Respondent was involved in
misconduct within the FHSA to submit to World Aquatics tampered invoices
in order to receive the subsidies of the OASP and also to deny athletes
reimbursement for all travel expenses incurred for their participation in
competitions.
62. Therefore, the Respondent’s conduct must be condemned in every way,
especially in view of the position she holds in Aquatics.
63. With respect to the length of the period of ineligibility, the Adjudicatory Body
notes that in a similar case of tampering with invoices in order to request
reimbursements from World Aquatics committed by the former President of
the Chilean Swimming Federation, the Adjudicatory Body imposed a 20-
year suspension on him.1
1 https://aquaticsintegrity.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/2024.02.29-Decision-of-the-AQIU-

64. Considering the above, the Adjudicatory Body is convinced that also in this
case it is paramount to issue a significant sanction to prevent such conduct
in the future and impose on the Respondent a suspension for a fixed period
of five (5) years from taking part in any Aquatic-related activities on behalf
of World Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World Aquatics
Member.
65. The suspension imposed on the Respondent shall also prevent her from
attending in any capacity, any aquatics International Competition, as defined
at Article 2.2 of the World Aquatics Competition Regulations. For the sake of
clarity, the Olympic Games fall within the definition of International
Competition.
66. Finally, the Adjudicatory Body observes that as per Article 21 of the Integrity
Code, the Respondent is as of 6 February 2024 provisionally suspended on
the ground that public confidence in the integrity of the sport of Aquatics is
at risk. In this regard, the Adjudicatory Body notes that, normally, the
suspension imposed should be credited for the months during which the
Respondent was provisionally suspended.
67. That being said, the Adjudicatory Body considers that, as the Respondent
violated the provisional suspension by acting as technical director of the
FHSA, the ten-year suspension shall be effective from the date this decision
is issued.

See also: CAS 2019/A/6344 Marco Polo Del Nero v. Fédération Internationale de Football
Association (FIFA) and CAS 2018/A/6072 Kwesi Nyantakyi v. Fédération Internationale de Football
Association (FIFA)

V. DECISION OF THE ADJUDICATORY BODY
(i) The AQIU has jurisdiction over this matter.
(ii) The Respondent has violated Articles 5.1, 5.2, 10.2 and 15.1 e) of the
Integrity Code.
(iii) The Respondent is sanctioned with a 5-year period of ineligibility
from taking part in any Aquatic-related activities on behalf of
World Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World
Aquatics Member and/or recognised body. The sanction begins on
the day this decision is issued i.e. 6 August 2024.
(iv) This decision is rendered without costs.
(v) As per Article 35 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code, this decision
can be appealed to CAS within twenty-one (21) calendar days of
the appealing Party’s receipt of the written reasoned decision in
question by email.
On behalf of the Panel of the Adjudicatory Body of the Aquatics Integrity Unit:
